title: Toward an Integrative Process-Based Framework of Psychological Experience.
abstract: Contemporary psychology and cognitive science have generated increasingly sophisticated accounts of cognition, emotion, behavior, embodiment, and neural functioning. At the same time, substantial fragmentation remains across explanatory traditions concerned with lived psychological experience, including constructivist, phenomenological, predictive processing, dynamic systems, affective neuroscience, and clinical process-based perspectives. The present article advances a process-oriented integrative framework intended to synthesize converging insights across these domains while clarifying how psychological experience may be continuously organized in real time across changing states and contexts. The framework proposes two dynamically interrelated generative processes-interpretive activity and experiential rendering-together with intrinsic regulatory potential, a hypothesized potential for reorganization. Interpretive activity refers to the ongoing organization of meaning through which situations, memories, bodily sensations, and anticipations become psychologically significant. Experiential rendering refers to the manner in which interpretations become experientially salient, emotionally compelling, and subjectively real. Intrinsic regulatory potential refers to the conditional capacity for broader, more flexible, and context-responsive reorganization as restrictive organization loosens. Related constructs include experiential authority, experiential constriction, experiential flexibility, state-dependent organization, and affect as directional signaling. Psychological distress is conceptualized not primarily as fixed pathology or static dysfunction, but as varying patterns of experiential organization emerging across changing states and contexts. The article situates the framework in relation to contemporary constructivist, enactive, phenomenological, predictive processing, and dynamic systems perspectives while outlining implications for psychotherapy, resilience, emotional wellbeing, and future process-oriented psychological research.
